There's no better way to defend our fundamental right to vote than by registering a ton of new voters and winning critical local, state, and federal elections. I am ten years old in Caracas when my mom asks what I think about moving to the United States. "No thank you," I say. All my friends and family are here. This is where I belong. I have never once considered the possibility of living somewhere else. I had already been to Disney World, so what more could America possibly offer? I don't give it much thought. Six months later, my mom tells me we are moving. I cry for weeks.
I am eleven years old in America. The plane ride is long, but I am not worried. I have my backpack stuffed with coloring books and my Game Boy. I press my face to the oval window and watch Venezuela disappear beneath the clouds, not fully understanding that I am watching it disappear from my life. For my birthday, my grandma gave me a journal. I love the embossed flower pattern on the cover and the navy elastic band that keeps it from falling open. "So you can write about your new adventure," reads the note inside. "I will miss you." I kept reading those four words the whole flight. I haven't seen my dad in weeks. He came ahead of us to find a place to live and to get things ready for our arrival, to find some version of a life we could step into. At the airport, my mom's eyes scan the crowd nervously until she finds him. His hair is longer than I have ever seen it. He looks thinner, too, or maybe just tired. They hug for a long time. I stand beside them holding my backpack, not sure whether to cry or smile, so I do a little of both.
Everything changed after that. A new language that lived in my mouth like gravel, words I had to practice in the mirror before school, sentences I rehearsed so I wouldn't be laughed at. A new culture with rules I couldn't always see. New friends who were kind but couldn't quite understand where I had come from, or what I had left behind. An unfamiliar, and at times unforgiving, landscape: strip malls and highways where I had expected something more like the movies. But also an opportunity: a path where the future held real options and room to grow, where my parents believed hard work would be met with something resembling fairness. It was not an easy choice for my parents to make. They left behind their careers, their friends, their language, the small comforts that make a place feel like yours. But it was a hopeful one, and a brave one, and I have never stopped being grateful for it.
I've spent a lot of time reflecting on this journey. There is a profound sense of loss that comes with leaving your home country, a grief that doesn't announce itself all at once but arrives in small, unexpected moments: a song on the radio, a smell that shouldn't remind you of anything but does, a phone call with your grandmother where you realize you've started to forget the right words. You become a person who belongs fully to neither place: never quite American enough to avoid the question of where you're really from, never quite Venezuelan enough for the family back home who have lived through things you only read about on your phone. Life moves on without you: the slang shifts, the inside jokes change, the relationships drift, until the place you feel homesick for no longer quite exists. It has become a version of home that lives only in you. You grow to love your new surroundings until they too become part of you, woven into who you are in ways you don't always notice. But you remain always aware that your roots are elsewhere, that you carry a connection that cannot and should not be severed, and that this doubleness, this in-between-ness, is not a wound but a kind of inheritance.
Five years ago today, I became a naturalized U.S. citizen. In the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic, I took the oath in a room with other hopeful new citizens, six feet apart, all of us masked, none of us touching. There was no fanfare. A government official read the words, and we repeated them, and then it was done. Fourteen years of paperwork, renewals, waiting rooms, and uncertainty collapsed into a single quiet moment. My family waited outside, straining to catch a glimpse of me through the thick bushes lining the USCIS building. I was handed a certificate and a small American flag to mark the occasion. I walked out into the afternoon light and immediately registered to vote. I was 25 years old, and for the first time in my life, I felt like I had arrived somewhere I was allowed to stay.
In 2016, I started speaking my mind about politics, about the state of the world, about the direction the country was headed: posting online, showing up to meetings, signing things, saying things out loud that felt dangerous to say. "Be careful," my parents told me. "We are guests here. It's not safe." I couldn't blame them for feeling that way. They had spent years making themselves small, learning not to attract attention, understanding that their right to be here was conditional in ways that mine, as a child, had never fully registered. Being an immigrant means navigating an endless maze of paperwork, scrutiny, and uncertainty, always one form, one missed deadline, one policy change away from having the ground shift beneath you. Citizenship changed that for me. It gave me a voice, and the legal right to use it. But the fear my parents carried didn't disappear with my naturalization certificate. The way people look at us, the way they talk to us: it has changed. And now we have a president who signals, loudly and without apology, that this kind of treatment is not only acceptable, but welcome.
That is what makes what happens tomorrow so personal. The Supreme Court will hear arguments in Barbara v.Trump, a case that could determine whether every child born in the United States is guaranteed citizenship -- a right enshrined in the Constitution for over 150 years.
On his first day back in office, President Trump signed an executive order targeting birthright citizenship, seeking to strip it from all babies born in the United States after February 19, 2025, to parents without permanent legal status. If the Supreme Court allows it to stand, the consequences will be immediate and devastating.
Ending birthright citizenship would deny U.S.-born children of non-citizen parents--regardless of their parents' legal status--the right to citizenship. This would leave many in legal limbo, creating a permanent subclass denied citizenship, legal identity, and fundamental rights. Even children whose parents hold legal visas could be subject to deportation, fracturing families and tearing apart communities.
President Trump has targeted immigrants since his first day in office, and his efforts to eliminate birthright citizenship are at the center of his cruel agenda to redefine who gets to be an American. But the 14th Amendment guarantees citizenship to children born in the United States -- and President Trump is not above the Constitution.
For more than 150 years, the 14th Amendment has been unambiguous: if you are born on U.S. soil, you are a citizen. That promise has protected millions of families and allowed new generations to put down roots, build lives, and secure a future for themselves and those who come after them.
I was ten years old when I didn't want to leave my hometown. I was twenty-five when I raised my hand and swore an oath to the country that had become my home. Birthright citizenship is not a loophole -- it is a promise, one that has made journeys like mine possible for millions of people across generations. Stripping it away does not make America stronger. It makes America smaller. That promise is worth defending.

I was ten years old when I didn't want to leave my hometown. I was twenty-five when I raised my hand and swore an oath to the country that had become my home. Birthright citizenship is not a loophole -- it is a promise, one that has made journeys like mine possible for millions of people across generations. Stripping it away does not make America stronger. It makes America smaller. That promise is worth defending. Thanks for reading By the Ballot! | | | | | | | Yen Bailey’s journey began with her parents, who fled war-torn Vietnam. Her father, a South Vietnamese Air Force pilot, bravely escaped the fall of Saigon by flying with his crew and dozens of Vietnamese refugees. They settled in Destin, Florida, where Yen and her brother were born and raised. Witnessing her parents' sacrifices and resilience deeply influenced Yen, inspiring her to pursue a career in law and public service.

[ ](https://yenbaileyforcongress.us9.list-manage.com/track/click?u=642870bb478010796c7288d8f&id=31e162c19b&e=58216231a8)

A Tallahassee-based attorney and Tulane University and Florida State University Law School graduate, Yen has dedicated her career to public service. She served as a Senior Attorney for the Guardian ad Litem Program and spent over 13 years as an ethics attorney at The Florida Bar. Committed to her family, Yen stepped away from her law career at the Bar to care for her elderly father.

Yen is a proud wife and mother. She cherishes time with her husband, Steve Bailey, a lawyer and professor at Florida State University and former Army Green Beret, and their two teenage sons.

Yen’s dedication to civic engagement led her to co-found Every Vote Florida, a nonprofit voter outreach organization, where she served as Vice President. She also served on the board of Friends of the LeRoy Collins Public Library System, promoting literacy and supporting public libraries in Leon County.

Yen is running for office to address the needs and challenges of the average Floridian in the panhandle. For years, many in the district have felt neglected and left behind by their Representatives, and Yen wants to be a voice for all in Washington D.C.

With her extensive background in public service and dedication to the community, Yen Bailey offers a fresh perspective for District 2. Her journey from the daughter of immigrants to a congressional candidate embodies the American dream and the power of perseverance.

Katie is up against a billionaire who’s poured **$101 MILLION** of his own money into his campaign, opponents funded by corporate cash, and the very real risk that two Republicans could end up on November’s ballot.
We _cannot_ fall behind. We’re up against the clock to raise the resources Katie needs to get her plan for an affordable California out there—single-payer health care, tuition-free public college, less expensive housing, free child care.

name: Save the Redwoods League
subject: We can't miss this moment for the redwoods
body:
Dear Peter,

Out in Harold Richardson Redwoods Reserve, there are ancient redwoods that have stood tall since the Middle Ages.

You can ensure they continue to stand tall by helping us expand this one-of-a-kind reserve. [https://secure.savetheredwoods.org/a/donate-hrrrexpansion] Will you help us make this acquisition possible?

My Gift to Expand the Reserve [https://secure.savetheredwoods.org/a/donate-hrrrexpansion]

We have a chance to add 200 acres to the reserve, safeguarding this land that is the ancestral home of the Kashia Band of Pomo Indians —who Save the Redwoods partnered with in 2024 to bring back forest-friendly prescribed burns to the property.

Expanding the reserve will also create a more resilient future for our region, safeguarding carbon-hungry redwoods that are some of our greatest allies in providing clean air and water.

This is an opportunity we cannot miss. Please join in and be part of ensuring these redwoods continue thriving for centuries to come. [https://secure.savetheredwoods.org/a/donate-hrrrexpansion]

For the Redwoods,
Save the Redwoods League

Make Your Gift Now [https://secure.savetheredwoods.org/a/donate-hrrrexpansion]

**Our end-of-quarter FEC deadline is just hours away, and we’re running out of time to close the gap on our $1 million goal.**

Roy Cooper

body:
The list of Trump’s illegal and unethical actions this month is looong. |
---
This March has been one of those months that has felt like it’s gone on _forever,_ Peter. In March alone:
* Trump started an illegal war with Iran with no plan for innocent civilians or American troops.
* Trump deployed ICE to airports to “ _help”_ with security wait times that are the direct result of his refusal to pass funding for TSA workers.
* The ICE Florence Correctional Center denied my visit to speak with detainees about their conditions and access to medical care.
* Gas prices have gone up more than $1 per gallon.
* Kristi Noem was replaced... with another inexperienced Trump fan.
* The FBI requested access to Maricopa County’s 2020 election records, trying to invalidate our free and fair elections.
* AG Pam Bondi continued to cover up the abusers found in Epstein files, denying thousands of survivors the justice they deserve.

The list can go on and on and on, Peter. But that’s the strategy of the Trump Administration. They throw everything they can at us to distract us and wear us out. _**But we can’t give in.**_ We have to remain hopeful and angry and committed to action. We have to lock arms and say, _we won’t stand for this._ We see this play out in big ways and small. The No Kings Marches. The fired up phone calls our office receives. The volunteers hustling to build support for candidates they believe in. Each and every one of us has the ability to make a real impact. We have already made a difference — and this November, when we usher in a blue wave here in Arizona and across the country, it will be because of our hard work. name: David Hogg
subject: Asking one more time, Peter

body:
Peter, I know I’ve been emailing
you a lot, but this is a make-or-break moment.

It may sound crazy, but right now young progressive candidates across the
country are watching and hoping that Leaders We Deserve meets our
end-of-quarter fundraising goal by midnight.

Why? It’s simple. Because the work we do at Leaders We Deserve is leveling
the playing field for every candidate we endorse, making it possible for
them to compete against the status quo even when their opponents are
backed by massive corporate PACs and shady special interests.

Everywhere I go, I hear it. I feel it. When I was knocking doors for
Christian Menefee in Houston earlier this month, people told me again and
again how glad they were Christian was in the fight. They were grateful
for the work we’re doing to make it possible for him to run and win.

Voters are hungry for change. But they’re sick and tired of being lied to
by the same politicians who have been involved in every major failure for
decades. They want a new generation of leaders who have walked in their
shoes and can actually represent them.

And those leaders are waiting in the wings, ready to step up. The problem
is the establishment is designed to protect itself. They have endless
money from corporate PACs, AIPAC, billionaires, you name it. And they try
to squash anyone who challenges them.

That’s why we exist. Because without Leaders We Deserve, many of these
candidates would not be able to overcome the odds that are stacked against
them. In 2024, our candidate Molly Cook won her state senate seat by 62
votes. This year, Akbar Ali won his assembly seat in Georgia by only 153
votes. These races are nail-biters — and our support makes the difference.

Right now, we have a critical end-of-quarter fundraising deadline coming
up at midnight. And our endorsed candidates are counting on our support
this year, so we really can’t miss our goal.

So I’m asking one more time,
Peter. Because your contributions power this
movement.

$3 now?

— David

| | | | High school dropout. Waffle House waitress. First woman to graduate from The Citadel. Single mom. Fighter.

Nancy Mace wasn’t born into power. She worked for every inch of ground she’s gained.

At 17, she dropped out of high school and took a job slinging hash browns at Waffle House to survive. No silver spoon. No Ivy League connections. Just grit, grace, and a whole lot of graveyard shifts.

By the grace of God, she turned that struggle into a story no politician can touch. She made history as the first woman to graduate from The Citadel, South Carolina’s legendary military college. She built her own business. She raised two kids on her own. And when the Left came for everything she believed in, she stood her ground. Now, she’s running for Governor of South Carolina.

Nancy Mace is a battle-tested conservative who’s walked through fire and come out swinging. In Congress, she’s been one of President Trump’s fiercest allies, fighting to secure our border, protect our daughters, and stop the Left’s sick agenda dead in its tracks.

She’s not here to make friends. She’s here to make history.

Nancy is fighting to:

* Eliminate South Carolina’s Income Tax—the highest in the Southeast

* Prosecute violent criminals and pedophiles with zero leniency

* Crack down on sanctuary sheriffs who let illegal aliens roam free

* Defund radical public universities that indoctrinate, not educate

* Reform education so students learn how to think—not what to think

* Work hand-in-hand with President Trump to put South Carolina FIRST

Through every hardship, Nancy never gave up. And now she’s ready to do what she’s always done: roll up her sleeves, take the heat, and lead from the front.

South Carolina is worth fighting for. And Nancy Mace is just getting started.

I want to share a bit about my personal life that you may not know yet.
I was raised by social justice warriors.
My dad marched for civil rights in Selma, Alabama, where he heard Martin Luther King Jr. preach.
My mom, born and raised in the Philippines, spent years fighting for the restoration of democracy in her home country.
They had me while living and working in the Philippines as social justice missionaries. I was born when a dictator was rising to power and martial law was imminent.
It was critical to both of my parents that I grow up in a country with democracy, freedom, rule of law, and human and civil rights — and sadly it became clear to them that wasn’t the case in the Philippines. So they brought my family here, to California, when I was just two months old.
A short while later, my parents began working with the United Farm Workers of America — fighting for workers’ rights, fair pay, and shade and water breaks alongside Dolores Huerta and Philip Vera Cruz.
I would never have guessed as a young kid that I would grow up to serve as the Attorney General of California — but as long as I can remember, I’ve known that I wanted to fight for those most vulnerable to have a fair shot at the California Dream.
That’s why I do this work. I know, without a doubt, that the California Dream is alive and well because I’m living mine — and I’m committed to using every bit of platform and power I have to lift people up and fight for justice for all.
I’m up for re-election in November, and I want nothing more than to continue this fight.
California needs an Attorney General who will stand up to those who abuse their power — whether it’s corrupt politicians, corporate polluters, extremist groups trying to roll back our rights, or powerful interests that exploit workers, cheat consumers, and put profits ahead of people.
So I’m asking you for help: Will you donate to my re-election campaign before our end-of-quarter deadline at midnight? clean_body: [] I want to share a bit about my personal life that you may not know yet. I was raised by social justice warriors. My dad marched for civil rights in Selma, Alabama, where he heard Martin Luther King Jr. preach. My mom, born and raised in the Philippines, spent years fighting for the restoration of democracy in her home country. They had me while living and working in the Philippines as social justice missionaries. I was born when a dictator was rising to power and martial law was imminent. It was critical to both of my parents that I grow up in a country with democracy, freedom, rule of law, and human and civil rights — and sadly it became clear to them that wasn’t the case in the Philippines. So they brought my family here, to California, when I was just two months old. A short while later, my parents began working with the United Farm Workers of America — fighting for workers’ rights, fair pay, and shade and water breaks alongside Dolores Huerta and Philip Vera Cruz. I would never have guessed as a young kid that I would grow up to serve as the Attorney General of California — but as long as I can remember, I’ve known that I wanted to fight for those most vulnerable to have a fair shot at the California Dream. That’s why I do this work. I know, without a doubt, that the California Dream is alive and well because I’m living mine — and I’m committed to using every bit of platform and power I have to lift people up and fight for justice for all. I’m up for re-election in November, and I want nothing more than to continue this fight. California needs an Attorney General who will stand up to those who abuse their power — whether it’s corrupt politicians, corporate polluters, extremist groups trying to roll back our rights, or powerful interests that exploit workers, cheat consumers, and put profits ahead of people. body:
Have you ever reached Easter Sunday feeling spiritually unprepared or wishing you had spent more time reflecting beforehand

| | | | [](http://e.goppresidential.com/rd/9z2z8bf3n6gojik3k200vf5qe77q464i9aus6n2iogg_rp22sh2s8i6epr5c1gm2o72cjh2bs)

Friend of Life, Have you ever reached Easter Sunday feeling spiritually unprepared or wishing you had spent more time reflecting beforehand? I know I have. Easter has a way of coming up fast. So before the services, before the plans with family, or the big dinner to follow, I wanted to share something my team created with you in mind. [**_He Is Risen: 12 Scriptures to Prepare Your Heart for Easter_**](http://e.goppresidential.com/rd/9z2zcj3brov3te07rbafmgo6beu7j9dj7d2t1a7iu48_rp22sh2s8i6epr5c1gm2o72cjh2bs) is a free devotional designed for the days leading up to Easter. It’s meant to be simple, steady, and grounding as you prepare your heart. Here’s what you’ll find inside:
---
* One full Scripture passage each day
* A short reflection to help you process what you’re reading
* A prayer to help you pause and respond

---
If you’re looking for a way to engage with Easter more thoughtfully this year, I hope this devotional serves you well. You can download your free copy here: [https://resources.preborn.com/he-is-risen](http://e.goppresidential.com/rd/9z2z7eamlgd96rh6ltmq0vhu1kkepun82nitoonqan0_rp22sh2s8i6epr5c1gm2o72cjh2bs) Wishing you a meaningful Easter season, Dan Steiner

Over the weekend, I went to the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This has been on my bucket list since I was a kid. I remember calling Space Camp myself, asking them to send brochures so I could pitch my parents on sending me. We did not have the money, so I did what a lot of kids did. I read everything I could. I watched anything related to space. I got hooked on science fiction. I fell in love with the idea that people would willingly climb into a machine, launch themselves into the unknown, and try to discover something new simply because it was there.
[Share The Angry Democrat](https://substack..cTvE0F2UodnSRDBK5R82CeBV0OBcpztr-bRTXNkaQKA?)
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/8db9e9ad-a7b4-4489-9049-cbdd4ddd5ff9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
My friends say I look like a Hawaiian Uncle
Walking into [Kennedy Space Center](https://substack.com/redirect/c9407c54-203c-42ba-85e2-66764407c27a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) brought all of that back immediately. The place itself is massive, thousands of acres of preserved land where rockets just happen to launch. It is clean, well maintained, and a little dated in parts. A lot of the experience is still built around touchscreens, videos, and guided storytelling. But then you turn a corner and see the real hardware. The rockets, the capsules, the scale of what was actually built. That is when it stops being a museum and starts feeling like something much bigger.
And that is where the experience shifts from nostalgia to something more complicated.
### The Apollo Mindset vs. The Modern One
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..my93EhgtrVIfBWJNGKkTGxvAACL8-kC-VqhtF3oANb8?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=192759034)
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..my93EhgtrVIfBWJNGKkTGxvAACL8-kC-VqhtF3oANb8?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=192759034)
When you walk through the Apollo section, you are not just looking at artifacts. You are looking at a mindset.
You see the control rooms from the early 60s. Solid desks. Analog switches. Landline phones. Rooms filled with engineers working through problems in real time. There is footage of John Glenn dealing with issues mid-flight, and you can hear the tension in the room as people try to solve it with tools that look primitive by today's standards.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/af58e0b2-1545-405a-b5da-d12ff92cc5e0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
[Replica of Mercury Mission Control from 1962 at Kennedy Space Station](https://substack.com/redirect/237152de-245d-49a3-87bf-adc6c600f34b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
And yet, they made it work.
They did not have perfect systems. They did not have certainty. What they had was urgency, belief, and a willingness to take risks that most people today would not even consider.
That is what struck me the most. The comparison between what they had and what they accomplished.
They were not doing it because there was something to extract from the moon. There was no oil. No gold. No immediate return. They were doing it because it mattered to try. Because exploration itself was the goal (well and beating Russia).
Now compare that to how we talk about space today.
One of the most common explanations for why we never went back is that there is nothing there. It is expensive. It is not worth it.
That framing alone tells you everything about how the mindset has changed.
We went from asking what is possible to asking what is profitable.
### The Price of Inspiration
There was another moment that stuck with me. It cost over $80 to get in, plus parking. $100! And that is before you even step inside. Standing there, knowing that this facility exists because of taxpayer investment, it felt off. Maybe there are operational reasons. Maybe the visitor experience is privately managed. But as a citizen, it felt like I was paying to see something I had already helped fund.
And the experience itself reinforces that feeling.
So much of it is packaged. Controlled. Delivered through screens and structured narratives. It reminded me of the [World Expo I talked about before.](https://substack.com/redirect/75115b76-6537-458c-97aa-f173d86c4401?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) There is something missing when everything is presented in a way that feels processed instead of lived.
And yet, the physical artifacts cut through that.
Standing under a Saturn V rocket, you cannot help but feel something. You start thinking about the scale of the effort, the number of people involved, the amount of coordination it took to make something like that work.
And then the question starts forming.
If we could do that then, why does it feel like we are hesitating now?
### Public vs. Private and the Shift in Incentives
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..my93EhgtrVIfBWJNGKkTGxvAACL8-kC-VqhtF3oANb8?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=192759034)
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..my93EhgtrVIfBWJNGKkTGxvAACL8-kC-VqhtF3oANb8?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=192759034)
The other thing that becomes impossible to ignore is how much of the current space activity is now driven by private companies.
As you go through the bus tour, you see launch pads and facilities not just for NASA, but for SpaceX, Blue Origin, Boeing. Old NASA infrastructure is being leased out. New systems are being built alongside the old ones.
In many ways, it is impressive. SpaceX, in particular, has driven down the cost of getting payloads into orbit dramatically. Reusable rockets. Frequent launches. A level of efficiency that changes what is possible.
[| | | | | SpaceX
---
@SpaceX
Falcon 9 launches 29 @Starlink satellites from Florida and completes the first 34th launch and landing of a flight-proven orbital class rocket
| 11:32 PM * Mar 30, 2026 * 208K Views245 Replies * 701 Reposts * 3.88K Likes
---](https://substack.com/redirect/1b0d9415-6088-4189-a2e2-07535c7acac3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
But it comes with a different set of incentives.
Now the conversation is about cost efficiency, payload economics, commercial viability. Space tourism becomes part of the discussion. Low Earth orbit becomes a marketplace.
And I do not think that is bad. In fact, it is necessary to scale what comes next.
But it does raise a concern.
If the primary driver becomes profit, what happens to the things that do not have an immediate return? What happens to the long-term exploration goals that require sustained investment without a clear financial payoff?
Because that is exactly what got us to the moon in the first place.
### What If We Never Stopped?
As I went through the exhibits, especially the Apollo section, I kept coming back to one idea.
What if we never stopped?
What if we treated that moment not as a finish line, but as a starting point?
There is a show I like, For All Mankind, that explores that exact question. What happens if the space race never ends? What happens if we keep pushing, keep investing, keep exploring?
[](https://substack.com/redirect/1e41b1b9-b7e6-453e-87c9-53245c59a2ac?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Walking through Kennedy Space Center, that question does not feel theoretical.
Because you can see both versions at the same time.
You see what we were capable of when we were driven by curiosity and ambition.
I left Kennedy Space Center feeling two things at the same time.
Inspired by what we can accomplish and what could have been.
Yet as I was leaving, there was Artemis II sitting on the pad, the first crewed mission back toward the Moon in over 50 years, (tentatively launching April 1, 2026) built through a mix of NASA leadership and private contractors, a reminder that we still know how to do this when we choose to, the question is whether we are willing to commit to it beyond just this moment.
Because the talent is still here. The technology is better. The capability has not disappeared.
If something does not have a clear return, it struggles to get support. If something is risky, it gets delayed. If something requires long-term commitment, it gets questioned.
And that is where I think we have lost something important. Exploration is not supposed to be safe. It is not supposed to be immediately profitable.
It is supposed to push us forward.

America went from chasing the impossible to questioning the cost | | | Apr 1 | | | | | | | | | | | | Over the weekend, I went to the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This has been on my bucket list since I was a kid. I remember calling Space Camp myself, asking them to send brochures so I could pitch my parents on sending me. We did not have the money, so I did what a lot of kids did. I read everything I could. I watched anything related to space. I got hooked on science fiction. I fell in love with the idea that people would willingly climb into a machine, launch themselves into the unknown, and try to discover something new simply because it was there. ? | | ---|---|--- My friends say I look like a Hawaiian Uncle Walking into brought all of that back immediately. The place itself is massive, thousands of acres of preserved land where rockets just happen to launch. It is clean, well maintained, and a little dated in parts. A lot of the experience is still built around touchscreens, videos, and guided storytelling. But then you turn a corner and see the real hardware. The rockets, the capsules, the scale of what was actually built. That is when it stops being a museum and starts feeling like something much bigger. And that is where the experience shifts from nostalgia to something more complicated. The Apollo Mindset vs. The Modern One When you walk through the Apollo section, you are not just looking at artifacts. You are looking at a mindset. You see the control rooms from the early 60s. Solid desks. Analog switches. Landline phones. Rooms filled with engineers working through problems in real time. There is footage of John Glenn dealing with issues mid-flight, and you can hear the tension in the room as people try to solve it with tools that look primitive by today's standards. | | ---|---|--- And yet, they made it work. They did not have perfect systems. They did not have certainty. What they had was urgency, belief, and a willingness to take risks that most people today would not even consider. That is what struck me the most. The comparison between what they had and what they accomplished. They were not doing it because there was something to extract from the moon. There was no oil. No gold. No immediate return. They were doing it because it mattered to try. Because exploration itself was the goal (well and beating Russia). Now compare that to how we talk about space today. One of the most common explanations for why we never went back is that there is nothing there. It is expensive. It is not worth it. That framing alone tells you everything about how the mindset has changed. We went from asking what is possible to asking what is profitable. The Price of Inspiration There was another moment that stuck with me. It cost over $80 to get in, plus parking. $100! And that is before you even step inside. Standing there, knowing that this facility exists because of taxpayer investment, it felt off. Maybe there are operational reasons. Maybe the visitor experience is privately managed. But as a citizen, it felt like I was paying to see something I had already helped fund. And the experience itself reinforces that feeling. So much of it is packaged. Controlled. Delivered through screens and structured narratives. It reminded me of the There is something missing when everything is presented in a way that feels processed instead of lived. And yet, the physical artifacts cut through that. Standing under a Saturn V rocket, you cannot help but feel something. You start thinking about the scale of the effort, the number of people involved, the amount of coordination it took to make something like that work. And then the question starts forming. If we could do that then, why does it feel like we are hesitating now? Public vs. Private and the Shift in Incentives The other thing that becomes impossible to ignore is how much of the current space activity is now driven by private companies. As you go through the bus tour, you see launch pads and facilities not just for NASA, but for SpaceX, Blue Origin, Boeing. Old NASA infrastructure is being leased out. New systems are being built alongside the old ones. In many ways, it is impressive. SpaceX, in particular, has driven down the cost of getting payloads into orbit dramatically. Reusable rockets. Frequent launches. A level of efficiency that changes what is possible. But it comes with a different set of incentives. Now the conversation is about cost efficiency, payload economics, commercial viability. Space tourism becomes part of the discussion. Low Earth orbit becomes a marketplace. And I do not think that is bad. In fact, it is necessary to scale what comes next. But it does raise a concern. If the primary driver becomes profit, what happens to the things that do not have an immediate return? What happens to the long-term exploration goals that require sustained investment without a clear financial payoff? Because that is exactly what got us to the moon in the first place. What If We Never Stopped? As I went through the exhibits, especially the Apollo section, I kept coming back to one idea. What if we never stopped? What if we treated that moment not as a finish line, but as a starting point? There is a show I like, For All Mankind, that explores that exact question. What happens if the space race never ends? What happens if we keep pushing, keep investing, keep exploring? Walking through Kennedy Space Center, that question does not feel theoretical. Because you can see both versions at the same time. You see what we were capable of when we were driven by curiosity and ambition. I left Kennedy Space Center feeling two things at the same time. Inspired by what we can accomplish and what could have been. Yet as I was leaving, there was Artemis II sitting on the pad, the first crewed mission back toward the Moon in over 50 years, (tentatively launching April 1, 2026) built through a mix of NASA leadership and private contractors, a reminder that we still know how to do this when we choose to, the question is whether we are willing to commit to it beyond just this moment. ## New SNAP Benefits Rules
Approximately 3.3 million Texans enrolled in the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) can no longer [purchase candy](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJyk0DHO4yAQBeDT4A4LCMb5C4o07rJbrrSNNZghRsIQwThObr9yrrDdSCN9eu_9uc93iCnmxy_Y0NI7lDnj0RISYf2eGZ51T9iW3UFuFbdSG85KKMOF5kLOHmL6zLrz1gn_Izu0chwHoeVFq2615iqM9ygdjGB8QI0BFxjMYEYHEq9dtCcmtJBSCiVNL0A55y4QAlyHHz0wLdBHKrWnFQnf0EL6lBfWfilbl-xK9GzscmNqYmo6jqPfWj5_TE2Y-d6YmlaERCtTU96pRoolMzV9Lb7s1PgC2X84ZM9b8cBDLRs_q3OHGUOk04DKbzf59zeZd1etfx4xpdjMyLR4bBDTNw7934gvq_4FAAD__wzoiTQ) or sweetened drinks using their benefits. The [new restrictions](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkL2OhCAUhZ8GOw0g_kxBsY3dbLuluchlJEEwXEZn3n4zJvsE2335cnJOcn7u8x188PHxDRvq8nJpjnhSwFIwXxhhz8-AtDwNRMq4pUw4Sy77mquai9mCD-9ZVVYbbm-iQi2GoeNKtEpWq-6wRQVSGu5cP_Zji8PYob310g5q4aby-lPGFRdCcCn6hoM0xrTgHIzdTXVMcbS-pNyUFQu-gFx4pwNzs6StCnotZSfWfjE5MTmd59msKzVXsHmkg8mJMB9-QWJycinZj4mw1x-uDUZ0vtCf3J95WYGwzkgl-6X4FKnK2u6nD8FTPzDFHxv4cM2X_512aPkbAAD__1dthB0), effective today, have been implemented in response to a state law passed last year and a waiver approved by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Texas is one of 22 states that have received a waiver to restrict the use of SNAP benefits. "_Texas is leading the way in aligning SNAP benefits with healthier food options_ ," Gov. Greg Abbott [said last month](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykUL3OnDAQfBrT7cneM1yucHEN3RcpVZQ0aA1rsGRsZJuP4-2j4xVSjDTSSPP3-2v4Ih98nH_Syqa-XRoiHyVwrZwvGmnLe-Ay7pZiybymXHhAiR1IDVINE_lwDrqZjJXTUzVs1OPRSq3uGpvFTJY6tK4drWVqqUVkeqhOP8nRON6x8eZjJrVUSklU3U0SWmvv5Bz9aJ-6FVry5GvKt7pw5TcVF870zfk2prUJZql1K-L-EtgL7I_juK0lfjSBPUfYi8B-YQp1EdjHvWZffYoC-882sBzZ-VqAMsO4UJx9nMFHuJKgMMOxUIUz7TBSvFDB7idQgeSAtuwDKIE9ZXi91N9f55-pyWbaDh-CL91DaDmv5MNVt_7fyd8G_wUAAP__6t2UTQ). The new rules prohibit using benefits for candy bars, gum, and drinks that contain 5 grams or more of added sugar, or any amount of artificial sweetener. Not everyone agrees with the changes. Lorna Ramage, deputy director of communications for the advocacy group Every Texan, [said](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLGyrCAMhp8GO5wQUdeC4jZ2e9tTOqBxZRbBAVx33_4M-wqny0zyf0m-n_t019ZZ__ivd1L5vYbJ05Uc5UzxW3p9xNNRmk-jfYq0h5hoQsCOg-QgpkVb95lktSgDyyAqUqLvW5CikVhtCuTQGDIdNI1YV2wBSHQD9qaTN1ratbKqwECCEAJQdDVoNMY0el31rR1kyyTQYnOIdd4o01un1X3Ci2I9h71yasv5SKz5x3BkOF7XVc_Ozk_cwply8GWK4Vh-YTh-8wzHspPhCA3DUdxKbtOZl65P3BMtPAf-9OHi2oQz8_OYw279gxchPFLK0c7ZBl9gVVTLcVnnbOp6JuGxa-u-1-W_OX0p_A0AAP__1DmMRg), "_We worry that these changes will lead to more Texas families going hungry, all while adding an unsustainable bureaucratic burden on Texas' small businesse_ s."
## Army 3D-Printing Barracks at Fort Bliss
The U.S. Army is building 10 3D-printed barracks at Fort Bliss to house over 500 soldiers deployed to the installation for the ongoing border security mission. It's the Department of War's [largest robotic construction project](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLuO8yAQhZ_G7ohgwPbvguJv3GXbLa0hDAkKBmsgt7dfJc0-wHZHOtK5fN_H9YgxxXz-wo1se4ayZnrURK0Rf2TGnW-J6unmMFemrXClFSSMQhoh1eoxptdqem-d9LPqyappGqRR2kB_saPxOAVnhlGBBqO0AlDOIwbCeR50H-07TBqplJKgxoNEcM5pDAH_DbMZOiPJx1b40C7U6Ik1pFe5Ex9OZeuTvbS2107_72DpYLmG8mz3t9XB8vtFfGZ2sITCTbgUaxWOCa9VnLncshclC-3FzjE38sIhM56utWfr90dMKdZx6ow8bxjTp7j9Ddfdwk8AAAD__xhigbs) to date. Surprise. Surprise. Instead of wealthy white liberals personally funding the cause they champion, the money came through public revenue streams tied in part to cannabis sales tax, property-related taxes, and other taxpayer-backed sources.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/35ac5573-f1d5-41ea-a8a6-3a3c973271b2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
In this episode of The Kathy Barnette Show, we break down what's happening inside the Republican Party--and why the SAVE Act, a bill requiring proof of citizenship for federal voter registration, may face resistance from within.

Is this political dysfunction... or something more deliberate?

Kathy walks through:

1\. What the SAVE Act actually does (and why it matters)

2\. Why passing it should be straightforward under Republican control

3\. The internal resistance building inside the GOP

4\. Whether this is weakness, strategy, or something else entirely

This is bigger than one bill. It's about whether those in power are willing to act--and what happens when they don't.

| | The first major test of this year for Democrats is not a congressional or senate race.

In April, the Wisconsin Supreme Court is back on the ballot, and MAGA has their eyes fixated on the court again.

You remember what happened last spring. Elon Musk dumped over $20 million into the race to try and buy the court. Democrats fought back, raising enough money from small dollar donations and outorganized the richest man in the world.

It embarrassed Trump so badly he threw Musk out of the White House and his role at DOGE. Then Elon and Trump had a public breakup, and Musk mostly vanished from politics for the rest of 2025.

But now, Elon is back... just in time for Wisconsin Dems to kick his ass again.

Just like last year, this race will set the tone for Democrats in 2026.

Defend Our Courts is suiting up for this battle. After our huge success in helping protect the PA Supreme Court in November, we are expanding nationwide. Wisconsin is our first major target and we are bringing the same winning formula forward.

The filibuster is one of the most distinctive and often misunderstood features of the United States Senate. Though frequently invoked in modern political debates, its origins and evolution reveal a procedural tool that has changed dramatically over time.
Contrary to popular belief, the filibuster was not part of the Constitution, nor was it intentionally designed by the Founders. Instead, it emerged in the early 19th century almost by accident. In 1806, the Senate eliminated a rule known as the "previous question" motion, which had allowed a simple majority to end debate. Without that mechanism, senators were left with the ability to speak for as long as they wished, effectively enabling unlimited debate on legislation.
For much of the 19th and early 20th centuries, the filibuster remained a rarely used tactic. When it did occur, it took the form of what is now called a "talking filibuster." Senators seeking to delay or block a bill had to physically hold the floor and continue speaking, sometimes for hours or even days. This made the filibuster highly visible and physically demanding. It was not enough to oppose a bill. One had to sustain the effort in real time, often under intense public scrutiny.
The first major attempt to limit this practice came in 1917, when the Senate adopted Rule XXII, establishing the cloture process. Cloture allows the Senate to end debate with a supermajority vote. Initially set at two-thirds of senators present and voting, the threshold was lowered in 1975 to three-fifths of the full Senate, which is 60 votes if all seats are filled. This change marked a significant step in balancing the Senate's tradition of extended debate with the need to eventually reach decisions.
However, the most consequential shift in the filibuster's history occurred during the 1970s with procedural reforms that allowed the Senate to consider multiple pieces of legislation simultaneously. This "two-track system" meant that a filibuster no longer brought all Senate business to a halt. As a result, the nature of the filibuster changed. Senators no longer needed to continuously speak on the floor to block a bill. Instead, they could simply signal their intent to filibuster.
This modern version is often referred to as a "silent" or "virtual" filibuster. In practice, it has transformed the filibuster from a physical act of endurance into a procedural requirement. Today, most legislation in the Senate effectively needs 60 votes to advance, even though a simple majority is sufficient for final passage. The mere threat of a filibuster is typically enough to trigger this higher threshold.
The distinction between the traditional talking filibuster and the modern version highlights how Senate rules and practices evolve over time. What began as an unintended consequence of a rule change has become a central feature of legislative procedure. Whether viewed as a safeguard for minority participation or simply a feature of Senate process, the filibuster's current form reflects decades of procedural adaptation rather than a fixed constitutional design.
Understanding this evolution is essential to understanding the Senate itself, a body where rules, norms, and traditions often carry as much weight as formal law.

I met with executives in Texas, Florida and Canada in the insurance, energy, and commodity industries and had the opportunity to speak at an event in Boston. While artificial intelligence capabilities continued to be a topic of interest, the focus among executives with whom I spoke had clearly shifted to the Iran War, geopolitics, and implications for agriculture prices, energy markets, inflation, and the midterm elections.
Best wishes for a thought-filled April!_**

| | **MARCH 1, 2026**

On February 22, 1980, a bunch of American college kids beat the Soviet Union in hockey. You know the story. The crowd went berserk, Al Michaels asked if we believed in miracles, and for one night, the Cold War had a scoreboard and the Free World was ahead. The video below is ESPN’s coverage of the last minute of that historic game.
46 years later, the United States beat Canada 2-1 in overtime to win Olympic gold for the first time since the big win in Lake Placid. Jack Hughes buried the winner. Connor Hellebuyck made 41 saves. While some might dismiss the event as “just a hockey game,” it was so much more...

| | **MARCH 8, 2026**

In March 2003, as the 101st Airborne rolled toward Baghdad, its commander—a two-star general named David Petraeus—turned to an embedded [Washington Post reporter](https://mansharamani.us4.list-manage.com/track/click?u=caf139d4582deef486da11685&id=ddf0033d1d&e=93b2c2b824) and asked for a glimpse into the future: _“**Tell me how this ends**.” _It became the most famous quote of the Iraq War, and eerily prescient. We invaded, toppled Saddam, disbanded the army, purged the government, and then spent twenty years (and a few trillion dollars) discovering that winning the war was the easy part.
And now, as the United States and Israel decisively move to put the final nails in the Iranian regime’s coffin, I can’t help but ask: “Are we destined to make the same mistakes we did last time?” On the surface, it seems we’ve learned a great deal. We aren’t pouring in troops or dumping in billions of dollars, and U.S. President Donald Trump doesn’t appear to have much appetite for nation-building or democracy-promotion. He even seems reluctant when it comes to regime change, instead suggesting the people of Iran should take on that project.
And yet, I am now asking myself the same question Petraeus asked 20 years ago: **How is this going to end?** So far, the military campaign seems to be progressing well, but it doesn’t seem like much thought has been given to what...

| | **MARCH 15, 2026**

Since the U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on February 28, many market prognosticators and geopolitical analysts have focused on casualties, disruptions to shipping, Iran’s erratic missile launches, and of course, the price of oil. Others have focused on the geopolitical implications of the war, how it’s impacting financial markets, and the possibility of politically problematic inflation during a midterm election year. I don’t mean to diminish the importance of any of these topics, but there’s another crisis unfolding that far too few people are thinking about: the impact of the Iran war on global food supplies.
The Strait of Hormuz is _de facto_ closed. The 21 miles of water connecting the Persian Gulf to the rest of the world has been deemed too risky for insurance companies to insure against loss given war risks. Shipping companies have stopped transiting through the area. As has been widely discussed, [about 20% of global consumption](https://mansharamani.us4.list-manage.com/track/click?u=caf139d4582deef486da11685&id=390a967cc9&e=93b2c2b824)passes through it. But so does LNG, to the tune of [about 20% of global LNG trade](https://mansharamani.us4.list-manage.com/track/click?u=caf139d4582deef486da11685&id=2e39fd7f1d&e=93b2c2b824).
What does that have to do with fertilizer? Natural gas is the primary requirement for ammonia, which is the building block for all nitrogen fertilizers. And natural gas isn’t just _part_ of the cost—it’s [70 to 90 percent](https://mansharamani.us4.list-manage.com/track/click?u=caf139d4582deef486da11685&id=7be8c426bf&e=93b2c2b824). This explains why Middle East countries...

| | **MARCH 22, 2026**

There has been a lot written lately about AI’s impact on the economy, specifically how many jobs it will eliminate. And that’s really only one of the many risks that will accompany the massive advancements in information processing capabilities that AI is empowering.
But there has also been a lot of discussion about the productivity boom AI will unleash, enabling massive breakthroughs in medicine and other research-driven fields. Scientists and many others have found the new found analytical capabilities very promising.

Today, I plan to dig deeper into the jobs-related impact of AI. And one of the most interesting ways to describe this dynamic comes from a person who I’ve had the pleasure of spending some time with at a crypto-related conference in 2019 – [**Eric Weinstein**](https://mansharamani.us4.list-manage.com/track/click?u=caf139d4582deef486da11685&id=09bf2f364f&e=93b2c2b824). Eric is a truly independent thinker and a fellow generalist...and recently summarized the job risk quite succinctly: **if your job has a name, AI will take it...**

| | **MARCH 29, 2026**

In the late 1990s, Lucent Technologies was America’s most widely held stock — a “picks and shovels” play on the internet revolution. The company lent billions to its own customers so they could buy more Lucent equipment. On paper, revenue soared. In reality, Lucent was financing its own demand. When the customers went bust, Lucent nearly followed. The playbook was simple: manufacture demand through vendor financing, book the revenue, let investors extrapolate, and hope no one notices the circular logic until the music stops.
Today, Nvidia invests $100 billion in OpenAI. OpenAI’s CFO acknowledges that “most of the money will go back to Nvidia.” Nvidia holds a $3 billion stake in CoreWeave, which has spent roughly $7.5 billion buying Nvidia GPUs — meaning every dollar Nvidia invested has boomeranged home. Nvidia even agreed to purchase $6.3 billion in cloud services from CoreWeave, effectively guaranteeing it would absorb whatever capacity CoreWeave couldn’t sell. When Morgan Stanley mapped the capital flows between just six AI companies, the diagram resembled a plate of spaghetti...

| | **MARCH 9, 2026**

Most observers are analyzing the recent activities in Venezuela and the US-Israeli strikes against Iran as isolated acts. Proponents note the world is safer without Maduro, the world’s leading supporter of narcoterrorism, and the IRGC, the world’s largest exporter of terrorism (a sentiment with which I agree). Opponents suggest these actions were brazen violations of sovereignty and will destabilize the world.
Both views may be missing the real story. When you step back and connect dots across energy markets, supply-chain dependencies, and the calendar of great-power diplomacy, a far more nuanced picture emerges: These moves may be the opening gambits in a grand strategy to strengthen Trump’s negotiating position with Beijing before his trip to China on March 31. Let’s **follow the oil** to see how this might be so.
China is the world’s largest importer of crude oil, bringing in roughly 11.5 million barrels per day. Despite their green posturing and climate “leadership,” the Chinese economy remains heavily dependent on fossil energy. Further, almost 40 percent of China’s oil imports have origins in the Persian Gulf and come through the Strait of Hormuz. Interestingly, 80 percent of Iran’s crude exports are bound for China, much of it via a “shadow fleet” of tankers designed to evade Western sanctions (not unlike the fleet used to ship Venezuelan oil to China). In short, two of China’s most important sources of discounted, sanctions-skirting oil were Iran and Venezuela. The Trump Administration just upended both...

On March 12th at 1230pm, Dr. Vikram Mansharamani spoke with Florence Gaub about the nature of Transatlantic relations, the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, the Iran War, and what Europeans think of Trump and America. Florence is the Head of Research for the NATO Defense College and is a bestselling author, advisor to many policymakers, and a friend! She’s also a thoughtful futurist, science-fiction buff, and avid surfer!
Specific topics addressed include:
* The need for Europe to become more self-reliant with respect to defense
* Russia as a domineering concern for most Europeans
* Why the world needs to focus on Trump’s actions, not his words
* The militarization of the Arctic and the strategic importance of Greenland
* America’s increasing focus on the Western Hemisphere and how it is being interpreted by the Europeans
* Why American troops in Europe are not nearly as important as the US nuclear shield and satellite intelligence
* How Europe (and NATO) thinks about the rise of China
* The political theater of leaders cozying up to Beijing
* How the Iran War may lay the groundwork for future conflicts

I'm a big Mets fan and am excited for the upcoming season. I think we're going to have a contending team despite/because of all of the changes. I attended Opening Day.
Yes, this feels frivolous. There's some part of me that is like, "Man, AI is going to kick off an automation [wave](https://substack.com/redirect/c4aa3f43-c4b9-44be-8cd0-d645d7b0f1c4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) unlike anything we've ever seen. How are you paying attention to sports at a time like this?"
Now, I know that's harsh. We all have to enjoy life and appreciate what we have while we have it. I find that I'm more effective when I'm positive.
But there's something that's gnawing at me that I'm going to try to express.
9 times out of 10 when we log on or turn on the TV, we are looking at the winners.
The State of the Union, our pro athletes, performers, actors, even influencers and writers. Most people we see and track are at the top of a pyramid, outliers and anomalies.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b91b5c49-d60d-415a-bdde-95a93d83415a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
It distorts our sense of what's happening.
Perhaps revealing of me - I have a grotesque fascination with pro athletes and celebrities who have gone broke. I watched a couple YouTube videos of this variety and now they get served to me all of the time.
If 10 million white-collar workers were to get kicked to the curb, what would we see change? In the real world, things would be different. The offices would be emptier and our neighborhoods bleaker. Maybe our neighbors would have to sell their house and our friends would need some help. Maybe we would too. But the media and social media we see would probably look just about the same.
One of my great learnings these past years has been that our media organizations are terrible at telling us what's actually going on out there. Our news networks have become chroniclers of the news-of-the-day in your preferred lighting and flavor. The American standard of living has slipped so far over the past number of years - a record 57% of us are pessimistic and 70% are having trouble affording a decent life - with very little meaningful genuine coverage. I sometimes think that instead of all of the hours of talking headery we are subject to, we should just get graphs and bar charts showing how we are doing free of distractions or commentary.
Yet our favorite anchors have to go out there and perform their task each night, and they're allowed few flare-ups or failures. It's a tightrope they walk, and they either become pleasant or inflammatory automatons or they get kicked off the rope.
I'm an anomaly myself now.
We are living in a K-shaped economy that is getting all the more extreme. Oracle just laid off 30,000 workers. What happens when the winners are vastly outnumbered by the losers, but the losers are invisible?
Studies have shown that being successful is less fun in a highly unequal environment. Even if you're at the top, you'd prefer that it gets spread around a little more. More people have to have a chance to win.

clean_body: I'm a big Mets fan and am excited for the upcoming season. | | ---|---|--- | | | Forwarded this email? ? for more | | ---|---|--- * | | | Apr 1 | | | | | | | | | | | | I'm a big Mets fan and am excited for the upcoming season. I think we're going to have a contending team despite/because of all of the changes. I attended Opening Day. Yes, this feels frivolous. There's some part of me that is like, "Man, AI is going to kick off an automation unlike anything we've ever seen. How are you paying attention to sports at a time like this?" Now, I know that's harsh. We all have to enjoy life and appreciate what we have while we have it. I find that I'm more effective when I'm positive. But there's something that's gnawing at me that I'm going to try to express. 9 times out of 10 when we log on or turn on the TV, we are looking at the winners. The State of the Union, our pro athletes, performers, actors, even influencers and writers. Most people we see and track are at the top of a pyramid, outliers and anomalies. | | ---|---|--- It distorts our sense of what's happening. Perhaps revealing of me - I have a grotesque fascination with pro athletes and celebrities who have gone broke. I watched a couple YouTube videos of this variety and now they get served to me all of the time. If 10 million white-collar workers were to get kicked to the curb, what would we see change? In the real world, things would be different. The offices would be emptier and our neighborhoods bleaker. Maybe our neighbors would have to sell their house and our friends would need some help. Maybe we would too. But the media and social media we see would probably look just about the same. One of my great learnings these past years has been that our media organizations are terrible at telling us what's actually going on out there. Our news networks have become chroniclers of the news-of-the-day in your preferred lighting and flavor. The American standard of living has slipped so far over the past number of years - a record 57% of us are pessimistic and 70% are having trouble affording a decent life - with very little meaningful genuine coverage. I sometimes think that instead of all of the hours of talking headery we are subject to, we should just get graphs and bar charts showing how we are doing free of distractions or commentary. Yet our favorite anchors have to go out there and perform their task each night, and they're allowed few flare-ups or failures. It's a tightrope they walk, and they either become pleasant or inflammatory automatons or they get kicked off the rope. I'm an anomaly myself now. We are living in a K-shaped economy that is getting all the more extreme. Oracle just laid off 30,000 workers. What happens when the winners are vastly outnumbered by the losers, but the losers are invisible? Studies have shown that being successful is less fun in a highly unequal environment. Even if you're at the top, you'd prefer that it gets spread around a little more. More people have to have a chance to win. Did you know reading books lengthens your life expectancy? Despite receiving a pardon from President Trump, these unjustly jailed men and women are still struggling to rebuild their lives after 4 years behind bars. Like Damon Beckley. After four years as a political prisoner, Damon came home to a life that had been completely destroyed. His family's landlord evicted them from their home, forcing his wife and son to live in an apartment with no heat. And Damon's health collapsed in prison after contracting MRSA and later requiring emergency cancer surgery. To make matters worse, Damon, his wife, and their son are now facing eviction and possible homelessness again. Sadly, Damon's story is far too common among J6 prisoners. In just the last 60 days, for help from January 6 families struggling to survive. Unless we can count on your help, we 'll be forced to TURN AWAY some of these desperate families. **FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE** Monday, Apr 1, 2026
**CONTACT** Barbie Harden Hall(352) 551-5762[barbie@barbieforcongress.com](mailto:barbie@barbieforcongress.com)
**BARBIE HARDEN HALL WILL QUALIFY BY CANDIDATE PETITION****TO REPRESENT FL-11** _Hall Looks to Build on Momentum, Swing District Blue_**(Lake County, Florida)-- Barbie Harden Hall has officially received the required number of verified candidate petitions for candidate qualifying to unseat Congressman Daniel Webster.** Even with candidate petitions being allowed from any Florida registered voter due to Republican attempts to redistrict, we are proud that **92% of the verified petitions are from the four counties that make up Florida’s 11th Congressional District--Sumter, Lake, Orange, and Polk.** This grassroots effort was also boosted by support across party lines with**over 25% of the petitions being submitted by Republicans, NPA’s, and Independent voters**.**Harden Hall** shared, “I am so proud to have reached this point with the support of volunteers throughout Central Florida that believe in this Campaign and believe it is time to retire Congressman Daniel Webster. So many have worked tirelessly to reach this goal--from retirees knocking doors in The Villages to 12-year-old Addisyn Meyer who singlehandedly collected over 250 petitions for me. Voters are increasingly frustrated with a Congressman that does the will of the President instead of what is best for them. Webster’s action, and inaction, are directly responsible for out-of-control costs, the unaffordability crisis, and the chaos in our federal government. Having reached this milestone, we will now put all power and focus into defeating him in November.”**Congressman Daniel Webster has been named Florida’s least effective member of Congress** by the Center for Effective Lawmaking for the 116th, 117th, and 118th Congresses, with only one piece of legislation signed into law in his nearly 15 years in Congress. Webster also missed 40% of the votes on the first day of the 119th Congress, proving his lack of care.As the Democratic nominee in 2024, Harden Hall swung the district 6.9 points to the left–the largest Democratic swing in the state of Florida. She is ready to use that momentum to flip this R+8 district.

name: Michele Tafoya
subject: Get. Back. To. Basics.
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Tafoya for Senate
body:
Folks – I’m curious if you feel the same way I do.
[](https://links.republicanemails.)Folks - I'm curious if you feel the same way I do.
Whether it's Joe Biden, Kamala Harris, Tim Walz, or insert any other far-Left career politician, doesn't it feel like they're constantly prioritizing fraudsters over families, spinning their wheels on useless projects, or making life harder for the rest of us?
They raise our taxes, force propaganda into our classrooms, give illegal criminals free stuff, and let their most extreme activists steer the ship...
[I plan to do the opposite - we're going to focus on getting things done and doing the small things right. Here's what I mean:](https://links.republicanemails.)

* Tell the truth
* Close the border and deport violent illegals
* Clean up our streets and punish criminals
* Expose fraud and root out waste
* Treat veterans like the heroes they are
* Cut taxes and lower costs
* Support voter ID in all 50 states
* Make government work better for you
* Use your tax dollars to benefit your life

**
**In other words, we 're going to get back to basics! **
**Nothing makes my blood boil more than a bunch of career politicians campaigning on big problems, getting elected, doing nothing for years - then campaigning on those same problems in the next election! **
**Rinse and repeat. Over and over again.**
**I have a hunch you 've seen it before. You're probably seeing those types of TV commercials every single day, mentioning the same problems we've talked about for generations.
You see, those empty promises drive me UP A WALL! I'm not like those phonies. I'm an outsider. I devoted my professional life to sports broadcasting and covering sports for the American people. I never even thought about running for office until I watched our country fall apart at the hands of these career politicians. That's why I jumped into this race.
[That's also why I'm in urgent need of some support.](https://links.republicanemails.)**
**I 'm not just running against two big-name, far-Left politicians - I'm also running against a system that rewards complacency, lack of curiosity, and going-along-to-get-along.**
**That 's not who I am. **
**And the questions I 'll be asking on the Senate Floor will ruffle some feathers to say the least. Which is why the far-Left is already shifting resources to Minnesota to destroy my campaign early. **
**[If we 're going to survive this, it'll be because of folks like you chipping in a few bucks here and there so we can stay on offense and win back this Senate seat.](https://links.republicanemails.)
I'm not asking for much - all I ask is for EVERYONE to pitch in SOMETHING (whatever they can afford) before the end of the month: | [PLEASE ADD $10
](https://links.republicanemails.)[PLEASE ADD $50
](https://links.republicanemails.)[PLEASE ADD $250
](https://links.republicanemails.)| [PLEASE ADD $25
](https://links.republicanemails.)[PLEASE ADD $100
](https://links.republicanemails.)[ANOTHER AMOUNT
](https://links.republicanemails.)
---|---
I can't do this without you. I mean that.

I sincerely hope you'll be willing to help. Regardless, I appreciate your time in reading this message.

Be brave. Do good.
- Michele
[](https://links.republicanemails.)
Michele Tafoya
Republican for Senate, Minnesota
* * *
[](https://links.republicanemails.-bF-tLveEqJQ9y5Ks182)
Imagine the look on Tim Walz's face when voters reject his handpicked candidate and elect a Republican for the first time in 20 years!
_That's what I 'm picturing..._
This is Michele Tafoya - I'm not a politician, and I've never run for office before.
But I made the decision to run for U.S. Senate because my state has fallen so far in such a short amount of time.
We have the opportunity of a LIFETIME to win, and I've never been one to give up when the going gets tough.
I have a hunch you aren't either.
[PLEASE DONATE HERE >>
](https://links.republicanemails.-bF-tLveEqJQ9y5Ks182)
| Paid for by Tafoya for Senate

| | Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw

Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18]

Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. Dear Partner,
We’re inviting you to join our monthly Partner Briefing tomorrow. In this meeting, the DNC team will cover:
* **Election Overview:** Topline election results and a high-level overview example on how the DNC has been supporting down-ballot races.
* **Coalitions Impact Event:** Provide key events the coalitions team has delivered, ranging from high-impact initiatives to bridging and broadening relationships with grassroots organizations and partners.
* **DNC Playbook:** Hear about the new tools the DNC has developed to help campaigns at all levels get started. Your input will help shape shared strategies, surface collaboration opportunities, and ensure early alignment.
* **Local Listeners:** Case study on the program and key elements on how we are rebuilding trust through deep community engagement.

He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal.
